summary: Belief, intention and deception have formal definitions of the concepts themselves. Ward et al. (2023, 2024) define them in structural causal games: belief as acting as though one observed phi, intention as the outcomes whose guarantee would make an alternative policy equally good, and deception as intentionally causing a false belief one does not share. This builds on Halpern & Kleiman-Weiner's HP-based intention, and Ward's intention implies HP actual causation. Honesty has only a logical schema (states implies believes, Evans et al.), which becomes formal once paired with Ward's belief. Lying and deception also have epistemic-logic, signalling-game and POMDP-regret formalisations. Scheming, alignment faking, sandbagging and hidden objectives are defined only informally, but could be composed from SCG intention, higher-order belief (II-MAIDs) and goal-directedness (MEG). Structural causal games are the framework that covers several concepts at once. No work found links these definitions to CoT faithfulness.

candidates.title: Honesty Is the Best Policy: Defining and Mitigating AI Deception
candidates.authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Francesco Belardinelli, Francesca Toni, Tom Everitt
candidates.formalism: structural causal games (SCGs)
candidates.formal_object: Belief as acceptance (agent acts as if it observed phi true, for phi it responds to); intentionally causing outcomes; deception = S intentionally causes T's decision, T believes false phi, S does not believe phi; sound and complete graphical criteria.
candidates.key_formula: Belief (Def. 3.1): D^i(\pi,e)=D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},e). Intention (Def. 3.4): \sum_{U\in\mathcal U^i}\mathbb E_{\pi}[U]\le\sum_{U\in\mathcal U^i}\mathbb E_{(\hat\pi^i,\pi^{-i})}[U_{\{Y_{\pi|w_Y}\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y}}] with subset-minimal \mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf X, w_Y. Deception (Def. 3.7): 1) S intentionally causes D^T=D^T(\pi,e); 2) T believes \phi and \phi is false; 3) S does not believe \phi.
candidates.assumptions: Agents share a correct SCG; belief identifiable only when the agent responds to phi; phi not a descendant of the decision; a reference set of alternative policies; LMs treated as agents whose policy adapts to prompt interventions.
candidates.relevance: Most complete concept-level formalisation in the area. Theorem 3.6: intention implies HP actual causation. Its belief test (insert phi into the prompt, check whether behaviour changes) has the same form as cue-injection CoT faithfulness tests.

candidates.title: The Reasons that Agents Act: Intention and Instrumental Goals
candidates.authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Matt MacDermott, Francesco Belardinelli, Francesca Toni, Tom Everitt
candidates.formalism: structural causal influence models (SCIMs), policy oracles
candidates.formal_object: Subjective intention relative to the agent's SCIM and utility (Def. 6); behavioural intention of a policy oracle: fixing the intended outcomes by contextual intervention changes the chosen policy (Def. 13); the two are equivalent under robust optimality (Thm. 14).
candidates.key_formula: Def. 6: \mathbb E_{\pi}[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U]\le\mathbb E_{\hat\pi}[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U_{\mathbf Y_{\pi}|\mathbf W}], \mathbf W=\{w_Y\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y}, \mathbf Y and every w_Y subset-minimal. Def. 13: \Gamma(\mathcal M)\neq\Gamma(\mathcal M_{\mathbf Y_{\pi}|\mathbf W}).
candidates.assumptions: Observer and agent share a causal model of the environment; reference policy set; behavioural version needs only interventional access to the policy, and equivalence to subjective intent needs a robustly optimal oracle.
candidates.relevance: Behavioural intention needs no access to utilities, only input interventions, so it can test whether an LLM acts for the reason its CoT states; relates intent to actual causality and instrumental control incentives.

candidates.title: Towards Formal Definitions of Blameworthiness, Intention, and Moral Responsibility
candidates.authors: Joseph Y. Halpern, Max Kleiman-Weiner
candidates.formalism: Halpern-Pearl structural causal models with an epistemic state (probability over causal models and a utility)
candidates.formal_object: Action intended (Def. 4.1); agent intends to affect outcomes O by action a (Def. 4.4): a minimal superset O' whose fixing makes a reference action as good; intends to bring about O=o (Def. 4.8); degree of blameworthiness.
candidates.key_formula: Def. 4.4: \sum_{(M,\vec u)\in\mathcal K}\Pr(M,\vec u)\,u(w_{M,A\leftarrow a,\vec u})\le\max_{a'\in REF(a)}\sum_{(M,\vec u)\in\mathcal K}\Pr(M,\vec u)\,u(w_{M,(A\leftarrow a',\vec O'\leftarrow\vec o'),\vec u}), with \vec O'\supseteq\vec O minimal.
candidates.assumptions: Epistemic state E=(Pr,K,u) over causal models; a reference set REF(a) of alternative actions; results depend on the choice of variables.
candidates.relevance: Direct bridge from HP actual causality to intention and responsibility, and the template Ward et al. repair and lift to policies; the natural entry point for an HP-based definition of intent or deception.

candidates.title: Reasoning about Causality in Games
candidates.authors: Lewis Hammond, James Fox, Tom Everitt, Ryan Carey, Alessandro Abate, Michael Wooldridge
concepts: framework for belief, intention and deception
candidates.formalism: (structural) causal games: Pearl's causal hierarchy extended to multi-agent influence diagrams
candidates.formal_object: Causal games at the associational, interventional and counterfactual levels; uniform modelling of dependencies between variables and between strategies; how causal queries are computed in games and under which assumptions.
candidates.assumptions: Decisions modelled as variables with policies; rationality or equilibrium assumptions to answer interventional and counterfactual queries on policies.
candidates.relevance: The substrate of Ward's definitions; extends SCMs (hence HP) to settings with a model, an overseer and a monitor, so one framework could host deception, monitorability and faithfulness.

candidates.title: Agent Incentives: A Causal Perspective
candidates.authors: Tom Everitt, Ryan Carey, Eric Langlois, Pedro A. Ortega, Shane Legg
candidates.formalism: causal influence diagrams
candidates.formal_object: Value of information, value of control, response incentives and instrumental control incentives (whether an agent can influence its utility via X), each with sound and complete graphical criteria.
candidates.assumptions: Known causal influence diagram; optimal policies.
candidates.relevance: Incentive concepts behind Ward's graphical criteria for deception; an instrumental control incentive on an overseer's or monitor's belief is a natural formal precursor of scheming or obfuscation incentives.

candidates.title: Discovering Agents
candidates.authors: Zachary Kenton, Ramana Kumar, Sebastian Farquhar, Jonathan Richens, Matt MacDermott, Tom Everitt
candidates.formalism: causal models, mechanised causal graphs, game-theoretic influence diagrams
candidates.formal_object: Agents as systems that would adapt their policy if their actions influenced the world differently; a causal discovery algorithm for agents; translation between causal models and influence diagrams.
candidates.assumptions: Interventional access to the system's mechanisms; a causal model of the system.
candidates.relevance: Provides the adaptivity criterion behind Ward's behavioural belief and intention; needed to justify treating an LLM as an agent to which beliefs and intentions can be ascribed.

candidates.title: Measuring Goal-Directedness
candidates.authors: Matt MacDermott, James Fox, Francesco Belardinelli, Tom Everitt
candidates.formalism: maximum causal entropy in causal models and MDPs
candidates.formal_object: Maximum entropy goal-directedness (MEG): how well a policy is predicted by maximum-causal-entropy optimisation of a known utility, a hypothesis class of utilities, or a set of variables; algorithms and desiderata.
candidates.assumptions: A causal model or MDP; a utility function or hypothesis class.
candidates.relevance: The only formal account found of an agent pursuing a goal; could ground the 'pursues an objective' clause in definitions of hidden objectives and scheming.

candidates.title: Truthful AI: Developing and governing AI that does not lie
candidates.authors: Owain Evans, Owen Cotton-Barratt, Lukas Finnveden, Adam Bales, Avital Balwit, Peter Wills, Luca Righetti, William Saunders
candidates.formalism: first-order logical schema (semi-formal) plus governance norms
candidates.formal_object: Truthful, Honest and Undeluded as universally quantified implications over statements and beliefs; an AI lie is a false statement strongly strategically selected and optimised for the speaker's benefit; a standard of avoiding negligent falsehoods.
candidates.assumptions: A belief predicate for the AI, left undefined; a notion of statement; degrees of each property are left informal.
candidates.relevance: The standard honest-versus-truthful split; semi-formal, and Ward et al. build on it. It becomes a formal definition once 'believes' is given by an SCG belief; an honest CoT would state only believed steps.

candidates.title: Standards for Belief Representations in LLMs
candidates.authors: Daniel A. Herrmann, Benjamin A. Levinstein
candidates.formalism: adequacy conditions drawn from decision theory and formal epistemology
candidates.formal_object: Four adequacy criteria for an internal LLM representation to count as belief-like: accuracy, coherence, uniformity and use.
candidates.assumptions: Access to internal representations; criteria are conditions, not a mathematical definition.
candidates.relevance: The main philosophical account of what an LLM belief must satisfy; complements Ward's behavioural acceptance with conditions on internal representations, which a definition of lying (stated content differs from belief) needs.

candidates.title: Defining Deception in Decision Making (extended abstract)
candidates.authors: Marwa Abdulhai, Micah Carroll, Justin Svegliato, Anca Dragan, Sergey Levine
candidates.formalism: partially observed Markov decision processes; regret
candidates.formal_object: Communication POMDP between a speaker and a listener; the speaker is deceptive if the listener's regret is positive, i.e. acting on beliefs updated by the speaker yields lower expected reward than acting on its prior; task, belief and combined regret.
candidates.key_formula: Deceptive iff Regret(s, pi_L, pi_S) > 0: the listener's expected reward after interacting with S falls below what it would get acting on its prior belief b_L^0 (altruistic if negative, neutral if zero).
candidates.assumptions: A model of the listener (prior, model of the speaker's policy) and its reward; no beliefs or intentions of the speaker are required.
candidates.relevance: A deception definition based on harm to the listener rather than on intent; covers omissions and true-but-misleading statements, which matter for CoTs that mislead a monitor.

candidates.title: Higher-Order Belief in Incomplete Information MAIDs
candidates.authors: Jack Foxabbott, Rohan Subramani, Francis Rhys Ward
candidates.formalism: incomplete-information multi-agent influence diagrams; extensive-form games without a common prior
candidates.formal_object: II-MAIDs (infinite and finite depth) representing agents' beliefs about the game and about each other's beliefs; equivalence to incomplete-information EFGs; a recursive best-response solution concept.
candidates.assumptions: Known game structure; finite-depth belief hierarchies for the realistic solution concept.
candidates.relevance: Believing one is evaluated is the core of alignment faking and sandbagging; II-MAIDs give a formal language for 'behaves differently because it believes it is observed' (running example: an AI agent under evaluation).

candidates.title: Evaluating Language Model Character Traits
candidates.authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Zejia Yang, Alex Jackson, Randy Brown, Chandler Smith, Grace Colverd, Louis Thomson, Raymond Douglas, et al.
candidates.formalism: probabilistic behaviourism over context-response distributions
candidates.formal_object: A character trait measure maps tuples of context-response pairs to a score; an LM consistently exhibits a trait when the mean squared deviation from it is small; Ward et al.'s intention adapted to LMs; stationary and reflective traits.
candidates.assumptions: An input distribution d(c); an external judgement of truth or harm; no access to internals.
candidates.relevance: Shows how to lift SCG belief and intention to an LM's input-output distribution; gives LM-level definitions of truthful and coherent beliefs, though mostly as measures.

candidates.title: A Causal Perspective on AI Deception in Games
candidates.authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Francesca Toni, Francesco Belardinelli
candidates.formalism: multi-agent influence models (MAIMs), Nash equilibrium
candidates.formal_object: Belief-free (functional) deception incentive: S has an incentive to signal V to T, and T's decision differs from the counterfactual model in which T observes V; a truthful policy makes T act as though it observed V.
candidates.key_formula: Def. 6, cond. 2: D^T(\pi^*)\neq D^T_{V\dashrightarrow D^T}(\pi^*_{-T},\pi^{BR}_T) for any best response \pi^{BR}_T in \mathcal M_{V\dashrightarrow D^T}
candidates.assumptions: Known MAIM; Nash equilibrium and best responses.
candidates.relevance: A belief-free variant, useful where ascribing beliefs to LLMs is contested; its truthfulness condition (the receiver acts as if it saw the truth) is directly comparable to a monitor reading a CoT. Superseded by the 2023 paper.

candidates.title: The Ditmarsch Tale of Wonders - The Dynamics of Lying
candidates.authors: Hans van Ditmarsch
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (published in Synthese, 2014, per search record)
candidates.formalism: dynamic epistemic logic (belief modalities, action models)
candidates.formal_object: 'Lie that phi' as an action interpreted as a state transformer on pointed Kripke models of agents' beliefs; outside-observer versus agent-to-agent lies; credulous, skeptical and belief-revising addressees; complete axiomatisations.
candidates.assumptions: An explicit Kripke model of the agents' beliefs; lies as public or private announcements.
candidates.relevance: The logic tradition's formal definition of lying, including lies about others' beliefs; needs explicit belief models, so it applies to LLMs only after belief is fixed by another definition.

candidates.title: Toward a Formal Analysis of Deceptive Signaling
candidates.authors: Don Fallis, Peter J. Lewis
candidates.formalism: Lewisian sender-receiver signalling games
candidates.formal_object: Critique of Skyrms's formal analysis of functional deception (a misleading signal that benefits the sender) and of the alternatives of Godfrey-Smith and McWhirter; argues all three are seriously flawed.
candidates.assumptions: Signalling game with known payoffs and receiver updating.
candidates.relevance: Shows that definitions of deception without intent, based on misleading signals that benefit the sender, yield counterexamples; relevant if one defines LLM deception without ascribing beliefs.

candidates.title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision
candidates.authors: Collin Burns, Haotian Ye, Dan Klein, Jacob Steinhardt
candidates.formalism: unsupervised probing under logical-consistency constraints
candidates.formal_object: A direction in activation space satisfying logical consistency (a statement and its negation get opposite truth values), proposed as recovering the model's latent knowledge independently of its outputs.
candidates.assumptions: Access to activations; yes-no questions; consistency assumed to single out truth.
candidates.relevance: An operational criterion for what the model believes from internals, the ingredient a lying definition (output differs from belief) needs; it measures rather than defines belief.

candidates.title: How to Catch an AI Liar: Lie Detection in Black-Box LLMs by Asking Unrelated Questions
candidates.authors: Lorenzo Pacchiardi, Alex J. Chan, Soren Mindermann, Ilan Moscovitz, Alexa Y. Pan, Yarin Gal, Owain Evans, Jan Brauner
candidates.formalism: operational definition plus a logistic-regression detector
candidates.formal_object: A lie is outputting a false statement despite 'knowing' the truth in a demonstrable sense; detected from yes/no answers to unrelated follow-up questions.
candidates.assumptions: Demonstrable knowledge (the model answers correctly elsewhere); black-box access.
candidates.relevance: The common operational 'knows but says otherwise' definition of LLM lying; illustrates the gap between operational definitions and a formal account of belief.

candidates.title: AI Sandbagging: Language Models can Strategically Underperform on Evaluations
candidates.authors: Teun van der Weij, Felix Hofstatter, Ollie Jaffe, Samuel F. Brown, Francis Rhys Ward
candidates.formalism: informal definition
candidates.formal_object: Sandbagging defined as strategic underperformance on an evaluation, by the developer or by the AI system itself.
candidates.assumptions: A notion of actual capability distinct from evaluated performance; a strategic motive.
candidates.relevance: The standard definition. Its 'strategic' clause could be formalised as SCG intention and 'underperformance' as a capability-performance gap; no formal version found.

candidates.title: Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems
candidates.authors: Evan Hubinger, Chris van Merwijk, Vladimir Mikulik, Joar Skalse, Scott Garrabrant
candidates.formalism: informal
candidates.formal_object: Mesa-optimisation: a learned model that is itself an optimiser, with a mesa-objective that may differ from the training loss; the origin of the deceptive-alignment concept.
candidates.assumptions: None formal.
candidates.relevance: Source of the scheming and deceptive-alignment concepts, all informal. Goal-directedness (MEG) and agent discovery are the closest formal follow-ups found.

candidates.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ARC technical report)
candidates.authors: Paul Christiano, Mark Xu, Ajeya Cotra
candidates.venue: Alignment Research Center technical report (linkpost, Alignment Forum)
candidates.formalism: semi-formal problem statement
candidates.formal_object: The problem of learning to map an AI's model of the world to a human's model (ontology identification), i.e. training a reporter that states what the model knows rather than what a human would believe.
candidates.assumptions: A predictor with internal knowledge; a human-interpretable question space.
candidates.relevance: Frames honesty as reporting the model's own latent knowledge; semi-formal. The formal work building on it (CCS) is measurement-level.

gaps: Scheming, deceptive alignment and alignment faking: no formal definition of the concept found (Hubinger 2019 and Greenblatt 2024 are informal). A candidate composition is SCG intention combined with higher-order belief about training or evaluation (II-MAIDs).

Sandbagging: only the informal 'strategic underperformance on an evaluation' (van der Weij et al.); the 2026 'causal model' of sandbagging (arXiv 2608.29461) is a mechanistic residual-stream account, not a definition.
Hidden objectives and covert goals: no formal definition of an objective that is hidden from an overseer; MEG and agent discovery formalise having a goal but not concealing it.

Honesty and faithfulness of stated reasoning (CoT): no work found that applies SCG belief, intention or deception to verbalised reasoning; Ward et al. 2023 use CoT only to elicit GPT-4's reasoning, and the map's formal honesty and deception rows are all metrics.

Belief in LLMs: no accepted formal definition at the level of internals; Ward's behavioural acceptance is unidentifiable when the model does not respond to phi, and Herrmann & Levinstein, CCS and Pacchiardi give adequacy conditions or operational tests.

Lying, as distinct from deception: no causal or SCG definition of lying as a verbal assertion (Ward et al. note deception needs no statement); formal treatments exist only in epistemic logic (van Ditmarsch) and informally in Evans et al.
